attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'all of your code' scope and 'as a result'. The 'if' clause states the causal condition rather than a forecast antecedent. The sentence is firm and categorical, not hedged.

contract.note: The plain reading (that full delegation causes no learning or skill gain) is ordinary. The contract rightly flags that the result depends on whether actively studying the generated code counts as delegation, and that 'developing code' is partly a matter of definition.

evidence.note: January 2026 RCT preprint: participants who fully delegated lost learning of the library compared with controls. This fits the claim's direction but does not show zero learning or a long-term lack of improvement.
Anthropic's write-up of the same study. How participants used AI mattered, the subgroups were small, and the authors make no causal or long-term claims. It does not settle the categorical wording.

reviews.rationale: The one study supports the direction: full delegation impaired learning. But it measures relative loss on an immediate quiz in small, non-randomized subgroups. It does not show that no learning or improvement happens, as the categorical wording requires. No evidence shows learning gains from complete delegation. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence and his own inference.

semantics.note: The drafter keeps the hedged inference ('suggests', rendered as 'probably'), which policy does not score. The firm 77% premise is folded in as a 'since' clause; it would need its own claim to be scored separately.

contract.note: The contract scores the hedged 'little organic demand' inference on a plain reading. Plain readings apply only to firm language. Organic demand also has no stated measure.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's FY2025 10-K: Microsoft about 67% of 2025 revenue; no other customer at 10% or more; the 77% top-two figure is for 2024. NVIDIA's 2025 share is not given, so the combined figure is not settled.
NVIDIA filing: $27B of multi-year cloud commitments, for R&D. Different company, metric and period; it does not measure CoreWeave's revenue share or organic demand.

reviews.rationale: The normalised claim's core is the inference that the figure 'suggests' little organic demand, which is hedged and so not scored. Even the firm premise is not settled: the 10-K gives Microsoft about 67% in 2025 and NVIDIA under 10%, so a combined 77% is unconfirmed but not ruled out. The 77% top-two figure belongs to 2024.

attribution.note: Zitron's own firm universal statement about AI startups.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal scope ('every single AI startup without exception') and both parts, margins and solution. The wording is firm, though 'solution' is vague.

contract.note: Gross margins and a 2025 comparison window are an ordinary reading of the margin-cost context. One qualifying counterexample refuting a universal claim is fair. 'Solution' remains loosely defined.

evidence.note: ICONIQ survey: average AI-product gross margins up from 41% to 45%, and 33% to 38% at the application layer. These are aggregate figures from varying samples, not a named startup's comparable margin series.
Replit's CEO says the company is gross-margin positive. This is a single unverified data point with no time series, so it does not show margins improving.

reviews.rationale: The survey averages point against a universal 'none improving', but they do not identify any startup with a comparable improving gross margin, which the contradiction condition requires. Replit's statement is a single point, not a trend. Nothing establishes that no startup improved. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He relays the Spotify CEO remark only as his trigger, not as the claim.

semantics.note: Keeps 'at all' and 'intentionally'. The statement is largely evaluative ('mindlessly', 'gassing up') but makes firm descriptive assertions about the tools.

contract.note: Reading 'replacing software engineering' as replacing overall engineering responsibility is an ordinary contextual reading. The March 2026 window and the bar requiring proof of design intent are evaluator choices that shape the result.

evidence.note: Anthropic disclosure, March 9, 2026: approval stays with humans, but agents find and verify bugs. A company's statement about its own tool, so it cannot establish the industry-wide claim either way.
February 2026 compiler demonstration in which agents do engineering tasks under human management. It predates the window and is a single demonstration.
2023 research showing RLHF can produce sycophancy. A possible mechanism, not proof of deliberate flattery in 2026 coding tools.

reviews.rationale: The packet has company disclosures and one demonstration showing that tools automate engineering tasks while humans keep approval. It has no representative workflow evidence on whether overall engineering responsibility is being replaced, and no evidence of intentional flattering design in the window. Neither condition is met.
